quote.translation: Kant, in his Lectures on Metaphysics, holds that what is absurd among the connections of things is blind necessity (die blinde Notwendigkeit), that is, fate (Schicksal), and blind chance (das blinde Ungefähr), that is, chance (Zufall); the former, he says, is "what is founded neither on the essence of the matter nor on other causes", the latter "what is contingent in every respect" (Kant's Vorlesungen über die Metaphysik, 2 Aufl. hrsg. v. Schmidt, S. 52 f.).

quote.translation: In the Critique of Pure Reason, too, he declares two propositions to be a priori laws of nature: that "nothing happens through blind chance", that is, "in the world there is no chance" (in mundo non datur casus), and that "no necessity in nature is blind", that is, "there is no fate" (non datur fatum).

quote.translation: He holds that both belong to the dynamical principles, though the former, as a consequence of the principle of causality, is to be understood according to the categories of relation, whilst the latter, which adds the concept of necessity to the determination of causality, is to be interpreted according to the categories of modality.

regions.text: の範職にって理解すべきであり後者は原因性の限定に加ふるに必然性の概念を以てする様相の範騰に従つて解釋すべきであるとしてある。なほカントがここで『偶然ばない』とか『運命はない』とか云つてゐるのは「世界には』ないと云つてゐるだけである。

quote.translation: Moreover, when Kant says here that "there is no chance" or that "there is no fate", he is saying only that there is none "in the world", and this "world" is nothing other than the so-called "world of appearances", or "nature", that is the object of mathematical natural science.

quote.translation: As he puts it, "these principles agree in that they permit nothing that would bring interruption and hindrance to the understanding and to the continuous connection of all appearances, that is, to the unity of the concepts of the understanding, in empirical synthesis" (see Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, B. 280-282).
